metadata.title: ELECTRA: PRE-TRAINING TEXT ENCODERS AS DISCRIMINATORS RATHER THAN GENERATORS

problem.value: Masked language modeling methods generally require large amounts of compute to be effective.

evidence.quote: While they produce good results when transferred to downstream NLP tasks, they generally require large amounts of compute to be effective.

problem.value: Current pre-training methods incur a substantial compute cost because the network only learns from 15% of the tokens per example.

evidence.quote: While more effective than conventional language-model pre-training due to learning bidirectional representations, these masked language modeling (MLM) approaches incur a substantial compute cost because the network only learns from 15% of the tokens per example.

problem.value: Current pre-training methods raise concerns about their cost and accessibility due to large compute requirements.

evidence.quote: Most current pre-training methods require large amounts of compute to be effective, raising concerns about their cost and accessibility.

contributions.value: We propose a more sample-efficient pre-training task called replaced token detection.

evidence.quote: As an alternative, we propose a more sample-efficient pre-training task called replaced token detection.

contributions.value: We call our approach ELECTRA for Efficiently Learning an Encoder that Classifies Token Replacements Accurately.

evidence.quote: We call our approach ELECTRAfoot_0 for "Efficiently Learning an Encoder that Classifies Token Replacements Accurately."

task.value: language representation learning and downstream NLP tasks

evidence.quote: While they produce good results when transferred to downstream NLP tasks, they generally require large amounts of compute to be effective.

method_summary.value: The approach trains a generator G and a discriminator D jointly, where the generator produces a distribution over tokens using a masked language model.

evidence.quote: The generator can be any model that produces an output distribution over tokens, but we usually use a small masked language model that is trained jointly with the discriminator.

method_summary.value: The generator is trained with maximum likelihood to perform masked language modeling by predicting original identities of masked-out tokens.

evidence.quote: The generator is trained to perform masked language modeling (MLM).

method_summary.value: The discriminator is trained to distinguish whether tokens in a corrupted example match the original input data or were replaced by generator samples.

evidence.quote: The discriminator is trained to distinguish tokens in the data from tokens that have been replaced by generator samples.

method_summary.value: The combined loss function of MLM loss and discriminator loss is minimized over a large corpus of raw text, and the generator is discarded after pre-training.

evidence.quote: After pre-training, we throw out the generator and only fine-tune the discriminator (the ELECTRA model) on downstream tasks.
We evaluate on the General Language Understanding Evaluation (GLUE) benchmark (Wang et al., 2019) and Stanford Question Answering (SQuAD) dataset (Rajpurkar et al., 2016).
We evaluate on the General Language Understanding Evaluation (GLUE) benchmark (Wang et al., 2019) and Stanford Question Answering (SQuAD) dataset (Rajpurkar et al., 2016).
For most experiments we pre-train on the same data as BERT, which consists of 3.3 Billion tokens from Wikipedia and BooksCorpus (Zhu et al., 2015).

evidence.quote: Lastly, we explore other training algorithms for ELECTRA, although these did not end up improving results.

limitations.value: More analysis is required to fully explain the parameter efficiency of ELECTRA.

evidence.quote: We speculate that ELECTRA is more parameter-efficient than BERT because it does not have to model the full distribution of possible tokens at each position, but we believe more analysis is needed to completely explain ELECTRA's parameter efficiency.

future_work.value: Future NLP pre-training research should consider efficiency alongside absolute performance and report compute usage and parameter counts.

evidence.quote: We also hope more future work on NLP pre-training will consider efficiency as well as absolute performance, and follow our effort in reporting compute usage and parameter counts along with evaluation metrics.

future_work.value: Comparing MLM predictions of BERT and ELECTRA could be an interesting way to understand the differences between their encoders in future research.

evidence.quote: We think comparisons of BERT's and ELECTRA's MLM predictions might be an interesting way to uncover more about the differences between ELECTRA and BERT encoders in future work.
Code and pre-trained weights will be released at https://github.com/google-research/ electra

claims.value: ELECTRA-Small outperforms a comparably small BERT model by 5 points on GLUE and outperforms GPT.

evidence.quote: 2 ELECTRA-Small outperforms a comparably small BERT model by 5 points on GLUE, and even outperforms the much larger GPT model (Radford et al., 2018).

claims.value: ELECTRA-Large performs comparably to RoBERTa and XLNet while using 1/4 of the compute.

evidence.quote: Our approach also works well at large scale, where we train an ELECTRA-Large model that performs comparably to RoBERTa (Liu et al., 2019) and XLNet (Yang et al., 2019), despite having fewer parameters and using 1/4 of the compute for training.

claims.value: ELECTRA-Large outperforms ALBERT on GLUE and sets a new state-of-the-art for SQuAD 2.0.

evidence.quote: Training ELECTRA-Large further results in an even stronger model that outperforms ALBERT (Lan et al., 2019) on GLUE and sets a new state-of-the-art for SQuAD 2.0.
